```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(inferguidR)
```

This tutorial evaluates one operating point from synthetic counts and then
from scored observations. It runs offline and does not train a model. Define
the positive class, score direction, comparator and evaluation sample before
interpreting performance.

## Start with the four counts

```{r counts}
spec <- classification_spec(
  counts = c(tp = 40, fn = 10, fp = 20, tn = 130), cutoff = 0.5
)
result <- evaluate_cutoff(spec)
metrics <- classification_metrics(result)
metrics[metrics$metric_id %in% c("tpr", "tnr", "ppv", "npv"),
        c("metric_id", "value", "status", "denominator_value")]
```

Sensitivity (`tpr`) divides true positives by all events; specificity (`tnr`)
divides true negatives by all non-events. Positive predictive value (`ppv`)
divides true positives by all positive calls. These denominators differ.
A missing denominator produces an explicit undefined result, not a zero.
Aggregate counts identify one operating point; they cannot reconstruct a ROC
curve or a cutoff sweep.

## State how scored observations are evaluated

The following small data frame is entirely synthetic. The scores are declared
as probabilities of the positive class; the comparator includes observations
whose score is exactly 0.5. These are demonstration observations, not a held-out
validation set.

```{r scored-data}
d <- data.frame(
  id = seq_len(8),
  event = c(1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0),
  risk = c(0.9, 0.8, 0.4, 0.7, 0.5, 0.2, 0.2, 0.1)
)
scored <- classification_spec(
  data = d, truth = "event", positive_label = 1, negative_label = 0,
  scores = "risk", id = "id", cutoff = 0.5,
  direction = "higher_is_positive", comparator = ">=",
  score_scale = "probability", evaluation_split = "same_data",
  sampling = "unknown"
)
evaluated <- evaluate_cutoff(scored)
tab <- classification_metrics(evaluated)
tab[tab$metric_id %in% c("tp", "fn", "fp", "tn", "tpr", "ppv"),
    c("metric_id", "value", "status")]
```

A score's numeric range alone does not establish probability calibration. The
`score_scale` and `sampling` settings document assumptions; they do not validate
them. Predictive values depend on prevalence, and the event proportion in an
outcome-selected sample need not equal population prevalence. A prevalence
scenario is a separate modelling assumption, not an observed population rate.

## Missingness and uncertainty

The default missing-data policy is `error`. Choosing `missing = "exclude"`
changes the evaluated sample and must be reported. Repeated observations from
the same unit need an explicit cluster definition; treating them as independent
can give misleading uncertainty estimates. Consult `?classification_uncertainty`
for supported interval and resampling settings.

```{r result-details}
evaluated$status
evaluated$limitations
evaluated$uncertainty
```

A cutoff selected and evaluated on the same data can overstate performance.
Prespecify a cutoff or separate tuning and evaluation samples. Small synthetic
examples cannot establish transportability, clinical utility or a recommended
operating threshold.

## Keep the analysis record

```{r export}
path <- tempfile(fileext = ".rds")
saveRDS(spec, path)
restored <- readRDS(path)
stopifnot(identical(ig_hash(spec), ig_hash(restored)))
```

Use RDS for the classification specification: `ig_from_json()` currently
imports power and report objects, not classification specifications.
Retain the input definition, data provenance, result and software revision
alongside the exported record. The [getting-started tutorial](getting-started.html)
explains the package's typed outcomes and reproducibility workflow.

```{r session-information}
sessionInfo()
```
